core.text: Someone described by what they are about to do, or intend to do, gets **the future participle (the 'about to' word: venturus = about to come)**: *epistulam scrīptūrus sum* — I am about to write a letter; *mīlitēs pugnātūrī* — soldiers about to fight. It is the participle stem with -ūr- slipped in before -us -a -um, and it is active. Latin name: *participium futūrī āctīvī*.
English has no single word for it; we say *about to …*, *going to …*, *on the point of …*.
Participle stem + -ūr- + -us -a -um. With sum it makes a near future: factūrus sum = I am going to do.

invented.en: The soldiers, about to fight, take up their swords.

core.text: *Scrīptus* is **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudatus = praised)**, passive and past; *scrīptūrus* is active and future. The -ūr- is the whole difference: *laudātus* — praised; *laudātūrus* — about to praise.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 23) list the three participles in a grid: present active -ns, perfect passive -tus, future active -ūrus (and the future passive, the gerundive, -ndus). Their examples: *puer ambulātūrus*, *oppidum cāsūrum*, *puella flōrem carptūra*, *mīlitēs moritūrī*. A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) forms it the same way and it is active as usual: *profectūrus* — about to set out.
*Sum* has *futūrus* — about to be, the future (adjective *futūrus* = future). The participle with *eram* gives 'was going to': *petītūrus eram tabernam* — I was intending to go to the shop.

teach.title: Describing someone by what is coming
teach.say: A person can be described by what they are on the point of doing, and the word that does it is **the future participle (the 'about to' word: ventūrus = about to come)**. *Mārcus longam epistulam scrīptūrus est* — Marcus is about to write a long letter. English has no single word for it, so we say 'about to …', 'going to …', 'on the point of …'.

teach.title: How the word is made
teach.say: Take the fourth principal part, the one ending in *-tum* or *-sum* (*scrīptum*, *datum*, *nāvigātum*), take off the final *-um* and put *-ūrus* in its place: *scrīpt-ūrus*, *dat-ūrus*, *nāvigāt-ūrus*. The *-ūr-* is the whole signal; what follows it is the ordinary *-us* of *bonus*. *Sum* does it too: its fourth part is *futūrum*, so its future participle is *futūrus*, about to be.

show.say: futūrus — the stem futūr- with the ordinary -us behind it

teach.title: It agrees like any adjective
teach.say: The ending follows the person described, not the verb: *-ūra* for one woman, *-ūrī* for several men. *Aemilia fīlium suum vocātūra est*; *Puerī in hortō lūsūrī sunt*. The *sum* beside it changes to match as well — *est* for one, *sunt* or *erant* for several. The table below runs the same three endings on *futūrus*: *futūrus*, *futūra*, *futūrī*.

teach.title: Telling -ūrus from -tus
teach.say: *Scrīpta* and *scrīptūrus* begin alike and mean opposite things. *Scrīpta est* is **the perfect participle (the 'having been done' word: laudātus = praised)** — done already, and passive. *Scrīptūrus est* is not done at all yet, and active. Hunt for the *-ūr-*.

teach.title: Standing without sum
teach.say: It does not need *sum* beside it. On its own it sits next to its noun like any other adjective: *Puerī dormītūrī in cubiculum eunt* — the boys, about to sleep, go into the bedroom. And it can keep an object of its own: *flōrem carptūra*, about to pick a flower. *Sum* has *futūrus*, about to be.
